name: Honey mask (manuka)

lead: A manuka honey mask is honey from the manuka tree spread on the face and rinsed off, used to calm irritated skin and clear breakouts for a clearer, calmer complexion.

Proponents point to methylglyoxal, the compound credited for manuka's activity, and to antibacterial effects seen in lab studies. Honey has been studied in wound care, including early evidence of faster healing of partial-thickness burns. No acne studies were found.

paras: People apply a thin layer of manuka honey to clean skin, leave it on for a short period, and rinse with warm water, often once or a few times a week. It is used on its own or as part of a gentle routine. Users usually judge it by how calm and clear skin looks over a few weeks.

Honey is generally safe in food amounts, and honey is advised against for babies. Labelling and authenticity of manuka products are disputed, and grading systems such as UMF and MGO vary. As with any food product on skin, allergic reactions or irritation are possible in people sensitive to honey or bee products.

angle.text: Skincare fans apply manuka honey as a rinse-off mask to calm skin and clear breakouts, citing its antibacterial activity. Honey has been studied in wound care; no acne studies were found.

lead: A manuka honey mask is honey from the mānuka tree applied to the face, used by proponents for acne and skin calming.

Mānuka honey is made from the nectar of Leptospermum scoparium, native to New Zealand and coastal Australia; its activity is attributed in part to methylglyoxal and graded by systems such as UMF and MGO [1]. Honey in general shows antibacterial activity in laboratory studies and preliminary evidence of faster healing of partial-thickness burns [2]. Neither page contains clinical evidence on acne.

paras: Mānuka honey is graded by methylglyoxal content (mg/kg) and by the trademarked UMF scale [1]. The UMF Honey Association says roughly six times more honey is sold internationally as mānuka than New Zealand produces, and UK tests in 2011-2013 found most mānuka-labelled samples lacked expected non-peroxide activity [1].

Wikipedia reports preliminary evidence for faster burn healing, moderate evidence for post-operative wounds, and low-quality evidence for other wound types; several medical-grade honey products are FDA-approved for minor wounds and burns [2]. Honey is not recommended for infants under one year because of botulism risk [2].
No studies found. Wound-care studies of honey exist but concern burns and wounds, not acne [2].
